parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Think about what actually vibrates when a progressive sound wave passes - what is doing the oscillating at the source and in the air?
Hint 2: Frequency is a rate, so focus on how to count those vibrations in a standard time interval of one second.
parts.proper_answer: Frequency is the number of oscillations per unit time of the source, or of a particle in the medium, or the number of wavelengths passing a fixed point per unit time.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture what is oscillating**
Think of a progressive wave as energy travelling outwards while the material itself just vibrates back and forth. For sound, the loudspeaker cone vibrates and each tiny air particle nearby vibrates in the same way.

Step 2: **Turn count into rate**
Frequency tells you how fast that vibration repeats. So count how many complete oscillations happen in one second:
$$f = \frac{\text{number of oscillations}}{\text{time}}$$
That is the number of oscillations per unit time of the source or of any particle, which is also the number of complete waves passing a fixed point per unit time.

parts.label: (b)
hints: Hint 1: Look along the horizontal time axis in Fig. 4.1 and measure the horizontal length of one complete sine wave in cm.
Hint 2: Convert that cm length into a real time using the $250 \, \mu\text{s cm}^{-1}$ setting, then think how period and frequency are linked.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the period from the screen**
One full cycle on the trace spans 2.5 cm horizontally. The time-base tells you each cm is $250 \, \mu\text{s}$, so:
$$T = 2.5 \times 250 \, \mu\text{s} = 625 \, \mu\text{s} = 6.25 \times 10^{-4} \text{ s}$$

Step 2: **Invert to get frequency**
Frequency is how many of these periods fit in one second:
$$f = \frac{1}{T} = \frac{1}{6.25 \times 10^{-4}} = 1600 \text{ Hz}$$
That confirms the stated value.

parts.label: (c)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Maximum heard frequency happens at the instant the source motion is directly towards the distant observer, so recall how source speed in that direction changes the observed wavelength.
Hint 2: Set the observed $1640 \text{ Hz}$, source $1600 \text{ Hz}$ and wave speed $330 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ into the moving-source relation and solve for the source speed $v_s$.
parts.proper_answer: Using $f_o = f_s v/(v - v_s)$: $1640 = 1600 \times 330/(330 - v_s)$, giving $v_s = 8.0 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Choose the approaching-source formula**
When the source moves towards a stationary observer the waves are bunched up, wavelength is shortened and observed frequency rises:
$$f_o = f_s \frac{v}{v - v_s}$$
Here $f_s = 1600 \text{ Hz}$, $f_o = 1640 \text{ Hz}$ for maximum, and $v = 330 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Step 2: **Rearrange and calculate**
Substitute values:
$$1640 = \frac{1600 \times 330}{330 - v_s}$$
$$330 - v_s = \frac{1600 \times 330}{1640}$$
$$v_s = 330 - 321.95 \approx 8.0 \text{ m s}^{-1}$$

parts.label: (c)(ii)
key_concepts: circular motion component towards and away
hints: Hint 1: Imagine the circle from above - during each rotation the loudspeaker must at one time have its velocity pointing straight at the distant observer and half a turn later straight away.
Hint 2: Link motion towards to compressed waves and motion away to stretched waves to predict whether heard pitch goes up or down at each stage.
parts.proper_answer: The heard frequency repeatedly rises above and falls below 1600 Hz. Motion towards the observer gives higher frequency, motion away gives lower frequency, due to Doppler shortening and lengthening of observed wavelength.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Track the velocity direction**
The speed around the circle is constant but the direction keeps changing. Twice per orbit the line-of-sight component is largest: once directly towards the distant observer and half a cycle later directly away from the observer.

Step 2: **Link motion to pitch**
Moving towards compresses the wavefronts in front of the source so observed wavelength $\lambda_o$ is smaller and $f_o = v/\lambda_o$ is higher. Moving away stretches $\lambda_o$ so $f_o$ is lower. The observer therefore hears the frequency smoothly rise to a maximum of 1640 Hz then fall to a minimum, repeating every rotation.
